title: Animals around us: their daily habits and their homes

summary.text: Crows, pigeons, ants, geckos and spiders share our buildings, and leopards walk the edge of Mumbai at night. Each of these animals has habits, things it does again and again, like a crow calling at first light or a bat flying out at dusk. Many animals build homes, but most use them only to raise their young or to hide, not to live in all year. You will watch animals near your home, find their daily patterns, and test how ants keep to the same path. Some questions are still open, such as why house sparrows have become rare in some cities.
summary.art: A cut-away drawing of an Indian apartment building and its neem tree: a crow on a stick nest, pigeons on a ledge, a gecko by the tube light, an ant line on the wall, a squirrel on the wire and a child at the window with a notebook.

intro.hook: Stand at a window or a door for one minute, very still. Count every animal you can see or hear. Do not forget the tiny ones. How many did you find?
intro.text: Most people say 'two or three'. Then they look again. A crow on the wire. Ants on the wall. A pigeon on the ledge above. A spider in the corner. A gecko asleep behind the calendar. We think animals live far away, in forests and zoos. But some of them live in our walls, our trees and our kitchens. Each one has its own day. It wakes, eats, rests and hides at its own times. You can find those patterns by watching the same animal again and again.
intro.art: A child at an open window, eyes wide, with small numbered circles drawn around a crow, an ant line, a pigeon, a spider web and a gecko.

outcomes: I can say what a habit is, and give the daily habits of at least three animals I have seen, such as when they wake, eat, rest and sleep.
I can name animals that are active by day, by night, and at dawn and dusk, and give a reason why an animal might choose each.
I can describe at least six kinds of animal homes, such as nests, burrows, hives, webs, mounds and hollows, and say what each one is for.
I can name animals that live in Indian towns, villages and forests, and explain why many of them live near people.
I can watch one animal for a week, write down the times and what it does, and find a pattern in my notes.
I can run a fair test about an animal habit, and say my claim, my evidence and my reasoning.
I can treat animals kindly while I watch them, and explain why we should not disturb a nest.
I can say what scientists agree about animal habits and homes, and what they still do not know, such as how birds find their way on long journeys.

terms.meaning: A living thing that must eat other living things to live. Most animals can move about on their own. People are animals too.
terms.example: A crow, an ant, a cow, a fish and you are all animals.
terms.art: A row of silhouettes: an ant, a crow, a cow, a fish and a child, all the same size.

terms.meaning: Something an animal does again and again, often at the same time or in the same way.
terms.example: Crows call loudly at first light every morning. That is one of their habits.
terms.art: A clock face with a crow calling at the 6 o'clock mark.

terms.meaning: Everything an animal does: eating, resting, calling, building, fighting, playing and hiding.
terms.example: A street dog scratching, sleeping and barking are all its behaviour.
terms.art: A street dog shown four times: scratching, sleeping, barking and sniffing.

terms.meaning: A place an animal uses to sleep, hide, store food or raise its young.
terms.example: A honey bee's home is a hive. A rat's home is often a burrow.
terms.art: Four little pictures: a hive, a burrow, a nest and a web.

terms.meaning: A home that a bird or another animal builds to lay eggs or raise its young.
terms.example: A crow builds a nest of sticks in a tree. A weaver bird weaves one from grass.
terms.art: A crow's stick nest and a hanging grass nest of a weaver bird side by side.

terms.meaning: A hole or tunnel that an animal digs in the ground to live in.
terms.example: Rats, porcupines and many crabs dig burrows. Many snakes hide in burrows that other animals dug.
terms.art: A cut-away of soil with a tunnel and a rat curled up at the end.

terms.meaning: The home of honey bees, made of wax rooms called cells.
terms.example: Giant rock bees often hang their hive under a water tank or a bridge.
terms.art: A big hanging honeycomb under a concrete water tank, covered with bees.

terms.meaning: A place where birds or bats rest or sleep together. It is also the word for resting there.
terms.example: In the evening hundreds of crows fly to one big tree to roost.
terms.art: A huge rain tree at sunset, its branches full of black crows.

terms.meaning: Active at night and resting in the day.
terms.example: Owls, fruit bats and house geckos are nocturnal.
terms.art: An owl and a fruit bat under a crescent moon.

terms.meaning: Active in the day and resting at night.
terms.example: Squirrels, crows and butterflies are diurnal. So are most people.
terms.art: A squirrel and a crow under a bright sun.

terms.meaning: Most active at dawn and dusk, the dim times just before sunrise and just after sunset.
terms.example: Many mosquitoes, and deer such as the chital, are busiest at dawn and dusk.
terms.art: A deer and a cloud of mosquitoes against an orange sunset sky.

terms.meaning: An animal that lives on its own, without people feeding or keeping it.
terms.example: A crow, a squirrel and a leopard are wild, even when they live in a city.
terms.art: A palm squirrel on a city electric wire.

terms.meaning: An animal that people have kept and bred for a very long time, for food, work or company.
terms.example: Cows, goats, hens and pet dogs are domestic animals.
terms.art: A cow, a goat and a hen in a village yard.

terms.meaning: To travel a long way at the same time each year, and then come back.
terms.example: Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas to spend the winter in India.
terms.art: A V-shaped line of geese flying over snowy mountains.

terms.meaning: An area that an animal guards and keeps others out of.
terms.example: A magpie robin sings from the same branch every morning to say 'this patch is mine'.
terms.art: A magpie robin singing on a branch, with a dotted circle drawn around its garden patch.

terms.meaning: To watch something carefully and notice details, often writing them down.
terms.example: You observe a pigeon when you note what it does and at what time.
terms.art: A child sitting still with a notebook, watching a pigeon.

terms.meaning: A person who studies plants and animals by watching them closely where they live.
terms.example: Salim Ali was a famous Indian naturalist who studied birds.
terms.art: A man in a hat with binoculars and a small notebook under a tree.

terms.meaning: A quick way to count by drawing a line for each thing. Every fifth line crosses the other four.
terms.example: Each time a pigeon lands, you draw one line.
terms.art: Tally marks in groups of five next to a little pigeon drawing.

explanations.definition: A habit is a behaviour an animal repeats, often at the same time of day, in the same place or in the same way.
explanations.description: Much of what animals do follows a pattern. A crow wakes at first light and calls. A squirrel runs along the same wire every morning. Ants use the same path to the sugar tin. These repeated patterns are habits. You can only find a habit by watching more than once. One visit shows you what an animal did. Many visits show you what it usually does.
examples: House crows call loudly at first light, and fly to a big tree together at sunset.
A street dog often sleeps in the same shady corner every afternoon.
Ants walking to food follow the same line. Ants that have found food leave a smell trail on the way back, and the others follow it.
explanations.art: A crow shown at three times on a clock face: calling at dawn, panting in the noon shade, flying to a big tree at sunset.
explanations.context: This card explains the first big idea of this unit: animals have habits, things they do again and again.

explanations.concept: Day animals, night animals and dawn-and-dusk animals
explanations.definition: Diurnal animals are active in the day. Nocturnal animals are active at night. Crepuscular animals are most active at dawn and dusk.
explanations.description: Every animal has a busy time and a resting time. Its busy time helps it find food and stay safe. Scientists think one reason fruit bats fly at night is that hawks and eagles, which could catch them, hunt by day. House geckos are busy at night, and many wait near our tube lights, because insects gather there. In hot places like India, many animals rest at noon, when the sun is fiercest. Inside most animals, a body clock keeps time, even in the dark.
examples: Fruit bats hang in big trees all day and fly out at dusk to find fruit.
House geckos wait near tube lights at night to catch moths.
Squirrels and crows are busy all day and sleep at night.
explanations.art: A circle split into day and night: a squirrel and a crow on the day side, a gecko and a bat on the night side, mosquitoes at the dusk line.
explanations.context: This card is about when animals are busy. Some animals work in the day, some at night and some at dawn and dusk.

explanations.definition: A body clock is a timer inside a living thing that keeps a roughly 24-hour rhythm of waking and sleeping.
explanations.description: Shut a fruit fly in a dark box, and it still wakes and rests at about the same times each day. This is because some of its genes, the instructions inside each cell, switch on and off in a cycle that takes about one day. Three scientists, Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young, worked out how the genes that run this clock work in fruit flies. They won a Nobel Prize for it in 2017. Sunlight resets the clock each morning, the way you set a watch. You have a body clock too. It is one reason you feel sleepy at night.
examples: A rooster crows before sunrise, even before the sky gets light.
When people fly to a far country, their body clock is still on home time. They feel sleepy in the middle of the day.
Bright lights at night can confuse the body clocks of birds and insects in cities.
explanations.art: A zoom-in from a sleeping fruit fly into one of its cells, where a tiny clock face is drawn inside.
explanations.context: This card goes deeper. It explains how an animal knows what time it is, even without a watch.

explanations.definition: An animal home is a place used to sleep, hide from danger, keep warm or cool, store food or raise young.
explanations.description: Many people think a bird lives in its nest all year, like we live in a house. Most birds do not. They build a nest only to lay eggs and keep the chicks safe. When the chicks fly away, the nest is left empty. At night most birds sleep perched on a branch. Other homes are used all the time, like an ant nest or a beehive. Some animals, such as elephants and tigers, have no fixed home that they return to each night. They move around a large area. A tigress uses a hidden den only while her cubs are small.
examples: A crow's stick nest is used for about two months, then left empty.
An ant nest under the floor is used all year by thousands of ants.
A tiger rests wherever it likes inside its large area of forest.
explanations.art: Three panels: a crow nest with chicks, the same nest empty with a crow sleeping on a nearby branch, a tiger lying in tall grass.
explanations.context: This card explains why animals have homes, and corrects a common mistake about birds and their nests.

explanations.definition: Animals make homes by building, digging, weaving, spinning or finding a ready-made space.
explanations.description: Each home is made from what is around. A crow builds with sticks, and in cities also with wire and plastic. A baya weaver bird weaves a hanging nest from strips of grass. A tailorbird stitches two leaves together with spider silk and plant threads. Honey bees make wax inside their bodies and build rooms with six sides. Termites build tall mounds of soil and spit. A spider spins its web from silk made in its body. An owl or a parakeet moves into a hole in a tree that it did not make.
examples: A potter wasp makes a tiny pot of mud and lays an egg inside it.
A rat snake lives in a rat's old burrow.
Rock pigeons nest on window ledges, because ledges are like the cliffs their wild relatives used.
explanations.art: A grid of six homes: a weaver nest, a tailorbird's stitched leaves, a honeycomb, a termite mound, a spider web and an owl in a tree hollow.
explanations.context: This card shows the many ways animals make homes, from weaving and stitching to digging and spinning.

explanations.concept: Homes that control heat: the termite mound
explanations.description: In south India the termite Odontotermes obesus builds mounds taller than a child. For years, books said these mounds work like air coolers, with the termites' own warmth pushing air up a chimney. Then in 2015 a team of scientists measured air inside real mounds near Bengaluru. They found the mound breathes with the day. In the day, the thin outer walls warm up faster than the middle, and air moves one way. At night the walls cool faster, and air moves the other way. So the daily change from hot day to cool night moves the air through the termites' home. Scientists are still studying how this works in mounds of other kinds.
examples: Deep inside a mound, the temperature changes much less between day and night than it does outside.
Termites grow a fungus garden inside the mound, which needs steady warmth and damp air.
Some architects copy termite mounds to design buildings that need less air conditioning.
explanations.art: A cut-away termite mound with red arrows of air going up the thin outer walls in the sun, and blue arrows going the other way under a night sky.
explanations.context: This card goes deep into one animal home. It shows how a termite mound in India keeps its air fresh using day and night.

explanations.concept: Why so many animals live near people
explanations.definition: Towns and villages give some animals food, water, shelter and fewer enemies, so these animals settle there.
explanations.description: A tall building has many ledges, like the cliffs where wild rock pigeons nest. A market is full of food scraps for crows and kites. Insects gather at our tube lights, so geckos find food there. Rats shelter in drains and eat what people throw away. Animals that can eat many kinds of food, and are not too shy, do well near people. Animals that need quiet forests or one special food often cannot live in towns. Every town is a habitat, a place where some living things find what they need.
examples: Black kites circle over Delhi's markets and eat the scraps people throw.
Cattle egrets walk behind cows and buffaloes in village fields. The animals' feet stir up insects for the egrets to catch.
Rhesus macaques and langurs live in many temples and towns, where people leave food.

Greater adjutant storks nest in tall trees in villages near Guwahati, in Assam. Purnima Devi Barman, a scientist from Assam, worked with village women, the Hargila Army, to protect the nests, and the storks grew in number.
explanations.art: A busy Indian market street from above: kites in the sky, a cow at a vegetable stall, crows on the wires and a rat by a drain.
explanations.context: This card explains why towns and villages are full of animals, not just forests.

explanations.concept: Animals of towns, villages and forests in India
explanations.definition: Different places in India hold different animals, but many animals live in more than one kind of place.
explanations.description: In towns you meet crows, pigeons, mynas, palm squirrels, street dogs, geckos, rats, bats and many insects. In villages you also see cows, buffaloes, goats, hens, peacocks, egrets, frogs, snakes and weaver birds in the palm trees. In forests live tigers, elephants, sloth bears, hornbills, langurs and countless insects and spiders. Some animals cross the lines. Leopards live in Sanjay Gandhi National Park, inside the city of Mumbai, and walk out at night past people's homes. India has more than 1,300 kinds of birds, and bird watchers often find dozens of kinds in a single city park.
examples: Indian grey hornbills nest in old trees in Delhi and Mumbai, not only in forests.
Peacocks walk on the rooftops of villages in Rajasthan.
Elephants walk through tea gardens and villages in Assam and Kerala.
explanations.art: A wide map-like picture of India in three bands: a town with crows and dogs, a village with egrets and cows, a forest with a tiger and hornbills, and a leopard walking between them.
explanations.context: This card is a tour of the animals you can meet in Indian towns, villages and forests.

explanations.concept: Watching an animal like a scientist
explanations.definition: To study a habit, a naturalist watches the same animal again and again, at set times, and writes down the time and what it did.
explanations.description: Good watching is slow and quiet. You sit in the same place, at the same times, so the animal gets used to you. You write the time and what the animal does, not what you think it feels. 'The crow sat on the nest for 20 minutes' is a note. 'The crow was bored' is a guess. After a week you look for patterns. When is it busiest? Where does it go? Jane Goodall, an English scientist, watched wild chimpanzees in Tanzania from 1960 in this way, for years. She had no university degree when she started.
examples: Write: '7:10 am. Pigeon lands on ledge. Carries a twig.'
Watch at the same three times each day: morning, afternoon and evening.
Sit far enough away that the animal goes on behaving normally.
explanations.art: A child's notebook open on a windowsill, with a table of times and little drawings of a pigeon, and the real pigeon outside.
explanations.context: This card explains how to watch an animal for a week, the way real scientists do.

explanations.concept: Why some animals travel far: migration
explanations.description: Some animals live in two homes, far apart. Each winter, bar-headed geese fly from Tibet, Mongolia and Central Asia over the Himalayas to Indian lakes. Amur falcons stop in Nagaland on their way from East Asia to southern Africa. Scientists agree that they travel to find food and good weather. How they find the way is less clear. Birds seem to use the Sun, the stars, smells, landmarks and Earth's magnetism. How they sense magnetism is still argued about.
examples: Bar-headed geese fly over some of the highest mountains on Earth.
Lakhs of Amur falcons rest near the Doyang reservoir in Nagaland every October and November.
Finding the way is not only a bird skill. Some dung beetles in Africa keep to a straight line at night by the glow of the Milky Way.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study bird eyes
perspectives.explanation: A substance in birds' eyes, called cryptochrome, may let them sense Earth's magnetism using a strange quantum effect. Experiments on robins support this. It is not proven yet.
Birds may sense magnetism with tiny bits of iron in their bodies, perhaps in the beak or the ear. Some early studies of this did not hold up. So they keep testing it.

explanations.art: A line of geese flying over the Himalayas at night, with faint magnetic field lines and stars drawn in the sky.
explanations.context: This card is about animals that travel far every year, and the open question of how they find their way.

explanations.definition: Watching kindly means we look without harming, chasing, catching or scaring the animal, and without touching its home.
explanations.description: An animal near its nest is protecting its young. If we go close, it may leave the eggs to go cold, or it may attack us. Crows dive at people who walk under their nests in the nesting months. They are parents guarding their chicks. So we watch from a distance, keep quiet and never touch eggs or chicks. In our tests we only watch animals. We do not pick them up.
examples: Use binoculars, or sit at a window, to watch a nest.
Never feed wild monkeys. It teaches them to grab food from people.
After the ant trail test, wipe up the sugar and wipe the floor with a damp cloth, so the ants stop coming to that spot.
explanations.art: A child watching a nest through binoculars from far away, with a dotted line showing the safe distance.
explanations.context: This card explains how to watch animals without harming them or their homes.

explanations.description: Animals that live in cities face noise, bright lights and new foods. Some seem to change their habits. In the noisy Dutch city of Leiden, scientists found great tits singing higher notes than in quiet woods, so their songs can be heard over traffic. Some city birds now sing at night under streetlights. Scientists think some of these changes are learned, and some may be slowly passed on through families over many years. How much the city is changing animals is a new and growing question.
examples: Some city crows use wire coat hangers to build nests.
Mynas in towns eat food scraps from bins that village mynas never see.
In cities with bright lights, some birds start singing before dawn, earlier than birds in villages.
explanations.art: A small bird singing on a streetlight above busy traffic, with musical notes drawn higher than the honking horn lines.
explanations.context: This card asks a new science question: are cities changing the habits of the animals that live in them?

agreed.text: Many animals have regular daily habits, controlled partly by a body clock inside them.
agreed.evidence: Animals kept in steady darkness still wake and rest on a roughly 24-hour cycle. The genes that run this clock have been found, first in fruit flies.

agreed.text: Most birds use nests only to lay eggs and raise chicks, not to live in all year.
agreed.evidence: Bird watchers who follow nests see them used for a few weeks and then left empty. At night birds are found perched in trees or roosts.

agreed.text: Many wild animals live in towns and cities, because cities give them food and shelter.
agreed.evidence: Bird counts in Indian cities, such as the Great Backyard Bird Count, find dozens of kinds of birds in a single town.

agreed.text: Animals build homes from what they find around them.
agreed.evidence: City crow nests often contain wire, plastic and cloth. Crow nests in villages are mostly twigs. Bird watchers in Indian cities have photographed many such nests.

agreed.text: Watching animals quietly over a long time teaches us things that a quick look cannot.
agreed.evidence: Jane Goodall watched the same wild chimpanzees for months before she saw them make tools from twigs and grass stems. Until then, most scientists thought only humans made tools.

challenging.claim: Wild animals belong only in forests. Animals in cities are lost or out of place.
challenging.who: Many of us think this without noticing.
challenging.for: Forests do hold most of India's wild animals, and many animals cannot survive in cities.
challenging.against: Crows, pigeons, kites, palm squirrels and geckos have lived alongside people for thousands of years. Leopards live in Mumbai's park and some walk past homes at night. For these animals the town is home.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea that wild animals do not belong in towns.

challenging.claim: Animals do not think about their homes. They build them by pure instinct, like machines.
challenging.who: René Descartes, a French philosopher, wrote in 1637 that animals are like machines. Many people still believe something like this.
challenging.for: A young weaver bird that has never seen a nest can still weave one. Part of the skill is born in it.
challenging.against: Young weaver birds weave messy nests at first and get better with practice. Crows choose new materials like wire when twigs are scarce. So building is part inborn and part learned.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that animals build homes without any learning at all.

challenging.claim: House sparrows are disappearing from Indian cities mainly because of mobile phone towers.
challenging.who: A popular idea in newspapers and messages.
challenging.for: Sparrow numbers did seem to fall in some cities as phone towers spread.
challenging.against: There is no strong evidence that towers harm sparrows. Many scientists point to other changes. Modern buildings have fewer holes to nest in. Neat gardens have fewer insects for chicks to eat. And in some cities sparrows have not fallen at all.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular claim about why sparrows are vanishing, and what the evidence says.

challenging.claim: Snakes come to drink milk, so we should leave milk out for them.
challenging.who: A common belief in many parts of India, especially around Nag Panchami.
challenging.for: Snakes are often seen near homes and cowsheds where milk is kept.
challenging.against: Snakes eat animals such as rats, frogs and eggs. They come to cowsheds and homes to hunt rats. Snakes cannot digest milk well. Forcing milk on a snake can harm it.
challenging.context: This card is about a common belief about snakes and milk.

challenging.claim: Male baya weaver birds put blobs of mud inside their nests to make them heavy, so the wind does not swing them.
challenging.who: An idea from Indian bird watchers.
challenging.for: The mud is real. Many nests have blobs of wet mud stuck inside the walls.
challenging.against: Nobody has proven why. Others think the mud may help the male show off, or help the nest keep its shape. Scientists still argue.
challenging.context: This card is about a real puzzle: why weaver birds put mud inside their nests.

challenging.claim: We should feed every animal we see in the city, because it is kind.
challenging.for: Feeding can help animals in hard times, like a hot summer or a flood.
challenging.against: Feeding monkeys teaches them to grab food from people. Bread and sweets can make birds and animals ill. Clean water in summer is usually safer and kinder than food.
challenging.context: This card is about whether feeding wild animals in towns is always kind.

big_questions.q: If a crow builds its nest with wire from your house, whose home is the nest?
big_questions.hint: Think of the tree, the wire, the crow's work and the chicks.

big_questions.q: Is a city a natural place, or not?
big_questions.hint: Ants build cities too. Is an anthill natural?

big_questions.q: How does a bat know it is evening, deep inside a dark cave?
big_questions.hint: Think about the clock inside every body.

big_questions.q: Why do most birds sleep on branches and not in their nests?
big_questions.hint: What is a nest really for?

big_questions.q: If you watched a crow for one minute, what would you know? If you watched it for a week, what more would you know?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between what happened once and what usually happens.

big_questions.q: Do people have habits like animals do? What are yours?
big_questions.hint: When do you wake, eat and feel sleepy?

big_questions.q: Should people share their towns with monkeys, leopards and snakes? How?
big_questions.hint: Think of what each one needs, and what keeps people safe.

big_questions.q: A family of bar-headed geese flies over the Himalayas every year. Which country is their real home?
big_questions.hint: Can a home be two places, or a whole journey?

big_questions.q: How can a termite mound breathe without a single fan?
big_questions.hint: What changes between day and night?

big_questions.q: Are you a wild animal, a domestic animal, or something else?
big_questions.hint: People are animals. Who feeds and shelters you?

story.title: The Wire Nest
story.note: Imagined: Tara, her family, Murugan and these two crows are made up. True: house crows build nests with wire and plastic in Indian cities, dive at people who walk under their nests in the nesting months, pant in the heat, gather to roost at sunset, and are often tricked into raising koel chicks. The koel mother lays her egg in the crow's nest and the crows feed the chick as their own. The loud ku-oo call is sung by adult male koels.
text: In the last week of May, when Chennai was so hot that even the pavements seemed to sigh, a crow stole the wire from Tara's window.

It was a short piece of copper wire, left over from when Appa fixed the fan. Tara had put it on the sill. The crow landed, tilted its head, and looked at her with one shiny dark eye. Then it picked up the wire and flew straight into the neem tree outside.

'Thief!' said Tara. But she went to look. On a fork of the neem, level with her window, sat a lumpy bowl of sticks. Poking out of it were things she knew. A green toothbrush. Two of Amma's hair clips. A loop of white electric wire. And now, her copper.
'Our house is in that nest,' she told Amma. Amma laughed. 'Then the crow owes us rent.'

By the next morning, nobody was laughing. Mrs Iyer from the second floor came up the stairs holding her head. 'That crow hit me,' she said. 'Right here. I was only walking to the gate.' By evening the crow had dived at the milkman, and at Murugan, the watchman. Murugan stood under the tree with a long bamboo pole. 'Mad bird,' he said. 'Tomorrow I will knock that nest down. Then it will go and live somewhere else.'

Tara did not want the nest knocked down. But she could not say why the crows were attacking, because she did not know. 'If you want to argue with Murugan,' said Amma, 'you need more than feelings. You need to know.'

So Tara made a notebook. On the first page she drew a line down the middle. On one side she wrote TIME. On the other side she wrote WHAT THE CROWS DID. Murugan agreed to wait. 'One week,' he said, holding up one finger. 'Then the pole.'

Watching is harder than it sounds. On the first day Tara wrote only: 'Crow. Crow again. Both crows. Hot.' The crows looked the same, glossy black with grey scarves round their necks. But by the second day she could tell them apart. One had a feather on its back that stuck out like a bent nail. She called that one Nail. The other was a little bigger, and it always arrived with something in its beak. She called that one Builder.

Slowly she learned their day. At first light, about half past five, they woke the whole street with harsh calls. In the hot afternoon they sat in the shade with their beaks open, panting like tired dogs. One of them always stayed on the nest. Nail sat, and Builder brought food. At sunset both flew off towards the big rain tree by the temple, where hundreds of crows met, and the noise was like a market. Later, in the dusk, Nail came back alone to the nest.

On the fourth day, Tara wrote down the time of every dive. 7:40. 7:52. 8:05. 8:15. Then, in the evening, 5:30 and 5:45. She stared at the page. Every dive came at the same two times of day. And every dive happened in the same place: the short path from the building door to the gate, which ran right under the neem branch.

'Morning and evening,' Tara said slowly. 'That's when everyone walks to the gate. Milk, school, office, coming home.' The crows never dived at people on the far side of the yard, by the scooters. They never dived at people on the road. Only at people who walked under the nest. 'They're not mad,' she said. 'They're guarding something.'
On the fifth day she stood on a chair with Appa's old binoculars. In the nest, a wide beak opened, pink inside. Then another, and another. Chicks.

Tara took her notebook down to Murugan. She showed him the times, and the little crosses she had drawn on a map of the yard. He turned the pages for a long time. 'So if people walk round the other side, by the scooters,' he said, 'the crows will leave them alone?' 'I think so,' said Tara. 'Only until the chicks can fly. A few weeks.'
Murugan scratched his chin. Then he tied a rope across the short path and hung a piece of cardboard on it. In his careful capital letters it said: PLEASE USE OTHER SIDE. CROW BABIES.
Mrs Iyer complained that the other side was ten steps longer. But she walked it. And the diving stopped. Tara wrote that down too. Day 6: no dives. Day 7: no dives.

The chicks grew. Two were scruffy and grey-black, like small copies of their parents. The third was strange. It was bigger than the others, blacker and shinier, and it shouted for food louder than both of them put together. Nail and Builder worked from dawn to dusk to fill its open mouth.

One morning in June, a new sound came from the neem. It was not the croak of a crow chick. It was a loud, shrill cry, again and again, and it came from the big black chick. Amma came to the window with a dish towel in her hand. She looked for a long time. 'That is not a crow,' she said, surprised. 'That is a baby koel. In a crow's nest.'

She explained. A koel mother does not build a nest at all. She waits until the crows are busy, slips into their nest and lays one egg among theirs. The crows do not seem to notice. They feed the koel chick as if it were their own. When a male koel grows up, he sings the ku-oo, ku-oo, ku-OO call that every child in Chennai knows from the summer.

Tara looked at the big black chick, its beak wide open, and at Nail pushing food into it. She looked at the toothbrush and the hair clips and her own copper wire, woven into the walls of the nest. The nest was made of the neem tree, and of their flat, and of two crows' hard work. And a koel was growing up inside it. 'Whose home is it, then?' she asked. Amma did not answer. She stood beside Tara, and they watched together.

In July the cardboard sign came down, and the nest stood empty, as nests do when their work is done. But every evening Tara still watched the crows fly off to the temple tree. The next summer, early one morning, she heard a koel calling ku-oo from somewhere she could not see. She wrote it in her notebook. Time: 5:40 am. What I heard: a koel. Maybe one of ours.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the crows were not attacking at random. Tara found their habit only by watching for several days and writing down the time and the place of every dive. The pattern showed that the crows were guarding a nest, and it also showed a simple way for people and crows to share the yard. That is the heart of this unit: habits are patterns, and patterns only appear when we watch over time. The story also quietly asks what a home is, when a crow's nest is built from a neem tree and a family's lost things, and raises a koel's chick.
ask: Why did Murugan think the crows were mad? What did Tara find out instead?
How did writing down the times help Tara? Could she have found the pattern in one day?
What did the crows build their nest with? Why do you think city crows use wire?
The crows fed a koel chick as their own. What do you think about that?
Whose home was the nest? The crows', the koel's, the tree's, or Tara's family's?
