games.title: Who Lives Here?
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a memory card game about animal homes. Each animal card has a matching home card. Some animals have no fixed home at all.

printables.title: 16 animal cards and 16 home cards to cut out
items: Crow | stick nest in a tree, sometimes with wire
Baya weaver bird | hanging nest woven from grass
Rock pigeon | a flat nest on a window ledge
Honey bee | wax hive with six-sided rooms
Owl | hole in an old tree
Indian grey hornbill | tree hole sealed with mud
Fruit bat | hangs upside down in a big tree
Palm squirrel | ball of grass and fibre in a tree
House sparrow | a hole in a wall or a roof
Black ant | tunnels under the floor or soil

printables.title: 4 wanderer cards
items: Tiger: no fixed home. It rests anywhere in its forest area.
Elephant: no fixed home. The herd walks from place to place.
Street dog: a favourite corner, but no house it builds.
Bar-headed goose: one summer home and one winter home.

rules: Cut out the 16 animal cards and the 16 home cards. Shuffle them together and lay them face down in rows.
On your turn, turn over two cards and read them aloud.
If the animal matches its home, keep the pair. Say one thing the home is for, such as eggs, hiding or keeping cool. Then take a leaf token.
If they do not match, turn them back face down. Try to remember where they are.

Shuffle the 4 wanderer cards into the rows at the start. A wanderer has no home card. If you turn one over, read it aloud and keep it. Say why that animal does not need a fixed home, and take two leaf tokens.
When all cards are taken, the player with the most leaf tokens wins.

setup.art: Thirty-six small picture cards laid face down in neat rows on a mat, with a bowl of paper leaf tokens beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay all the cards face down in rows.

setup.art: A child turning over two cards: a picture of a weaver bird and a picture of a hanging grass nest.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two cards. Do they match?

setup.art: A child holding a matched pair of cards and taking a paper leaf token from the bowl.
setup.caption: 3. A match wins a leaf token.

flow.do: 1. Cut out all the cards and tokens. 2. Mix the wanderer cards in. 3. Lay all cards face down in rows.
flow.say: Every animal here has a home, or a special reason for not having one. Let's see who can remember where each home is hiding.
flow.kid: Lay all the cards face down. Every animal has a home card. Find the pairs!
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Lives Here?, a memory card game about animal homes. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play a practice round. Turn over the crow and the stick nest cards together.
flow.say: Let's practise. This is a crow, and this is a stick nest. In the city, crows often add wire. What do you think the nest is for?
flow.kid: Practice round. A crow and a stick nest. What is the nest for? Tap your answer.
flow.context: This is a practice round of Who Lives Here?, the animal homes memory game.

ask.q: Does the crow sleep in its nest every night of the year?
good: No. Only while it has eggs or chicks.
Most of the year it sleeps on a branch.

check.q: What is a crow's nest mainly for?
options: Sleeping in, every night of the year
Laying eggs and keeping the chicks safe
Storing food for the winter
check.why: A crow builds its nest to lay eggs and raise chicks. When the chicks fly away, the nest is left empty. Picking 'sleeping in every night' is the most common mistake, because we think of a nest as a bird's house. Picking 'storing food' mixes crows up with squirrels or ants.

flow.do: Play the game. After each match, let the player say what the home is for.
flow.say: Your turn. Turn over two cards. If they match, tell us what the home is for. Eggs? Hiding? Keeping cool?
flow.kid: Your turn. Turn two cards. If they match, say what the home is for.
flow.context: This is the main part of Who Lives Here?, the animal homes memory game.
flow.parent: Good answers: the termite mound shelters the termites from heat and keeps the air inside damp and fresh. The web is a trap and a resting place. The hornbill's sealed hole keeps the mother and chicks safe from snakes and monkeys.

flow.do: When someone turns over a wanderer card, stop and talk about it.
flow.say: A wanderer! The tiger has no fixed home. Why might a big animal like a tiger keep moving?
flow.kid: A wanderer card! This animal has no fixed home. Why not? Tap your answer.
flow.context: This step of the Who Lives Here? game is about animals that have no fixed home.

check.q: Why does a tiger have no fixed home?
options: It is too lazy to build one.
It needs a big area to find enough food, so it keeps moving.
Tigers are never tired, so they never rest.
check.why: A tiger eats large animals like deer. One small patch of forest does not have enough deer, so it roams a big area and rests wherever it is. Picking 'lazy' means thinking every animal should build a home like ours. Tigers do rest, for many hours a day.

flow.do: Count the leaf tokens. Ask the closing question.
flow.say: Count your leaves. Now think. Which home was the cleverest, and why?
flow.kid: Count your leaf tokens. Which home was the cleverest? Say why.
flow.context: This is the last step of Who Lives Here?, the animal homes memory game.
flow.think: Which animal home near your house could you go and look at tomorrow?

games.title: Day Shift, Night Shift
games.players: 2 or more players, best with 3 or more. One child can play with the app calling.
games.context: This is a running and sorting game about when animals are busy. Players run to the day side, the night side or the middle line for dawn and dusk.

printables.title: Three signs for the floor
items: SUNSET LINE: dawn and dusk animals (crepuscular)

rules: Put the SUN sign at one end of the room and the MOON sign at the other end. Put the SUNSET LINE in the middle, on a strip of tape or a dupatta.
The caller reads one animal card aloud.
Everyone runs to the sign for when that animal is busiest: SUN, MOON or the SUNSET LINE.
The caller reads the answer on the back. Everyone who was right scores a point.
Anyone who can say why that animal is busy at that time scores a bonus point.
After 12 cards, swap the caller. The player with the most points wins.

setup.art: A room with a paper sun taped to one wall, a paper moon on the opposite wall and an orange dupatta on the floor in between.
setup.caption: 1. Put the sun, the moon and the sunset line in place.

setup.art: A parent holding up a card with an owl drawing while three children run towards the moon sign.
setup.caption: 2. Hear the animal. Run to its busy time.

setup.art: Children standing at the sun, the moon and the middle line, with one child explaining with her hands.
setup.caption: 3. Say why, for a bonus point.

flow.do: 1. Tape the SUN sign to one wall and the MOON sign to the opposite wall. 2. Lay a dupatta across the middle of the floor. 3. Shuffle the cards.
flow.say: Some animals work the day shift, some work the night shift, and some work at dawn and dusk. When I call an animal, run to its shift.
flow.kid: Sun is for day animals. Moon is for night animals. The middle line is for dawn and dusk. Get ready to run!
flow.context: This is the first step of Day Shift, Night Shift, a running game about when animals are busy. Here you set up the room.

flow.do: Call 'Owl' as the practice card.
flow.say: Owl! Where do you run?
flow.kid: Owl! Where do you go? Tap your answer.
flow.context: This is the practice round of Day Shift, Night Shift, the game about when animals are busy.

options: In the day, under the sun
At night, under the moon
Only at noon
check.why: Most owls hunt at night. Their big eyes gather dim light, and their soft feathers make no sound, so mice do not hear them coming. A few owls, like the spotted owlet, are also seen at dusk. Picking 'day' usually means mixing owls up with eagles and kites, which hunt in daylight.

flow.do: Call the cards one by one. After each, read the answer and let children explain.
flow.say: Next animal: fruit bat! Run! Now, who can tell me why bats come out in the evening?
flow.kid: Listen to the next animal. Run to its shift. Then say why.
flow.context: This is the main part of Day Shift, Night Shift, the game about when animals are busy.
flow.parent: Answers: day for crow, squirrel, butterfly, pigeon, honey bee, myna, kingfisher, rooster and bulbul. Night for owl, fruit bat, gecko, firefly, cockroach, jackal, moth, rat, night heron and frog (most frogs call after dark). Earthworms are night animals too: they come up when the ground is cool and damp. Dawn and dusk for mosquito and deer. Tigers and leopards hunt at night and at dawn and dusk, so both MOON and the line can be right. Accept good reasons.

flow.do: Stop and ask the big question.
flow.say: Many animals rest at noon and are busy at dawn and dusk. Why do you think that is? Think of heat, light and enemies.
flow.kid: Why are many animals busy at dawn and dusk? Tap the best reason.
flow.context: This step of Day Shift, Night Shift asks why animals choose a time to be busy.

check.q: Why are many Indian animals busy at dawn and dusk, but resting at noon?
options: Noon is too hot, and dawn and dusk are cooler.
They cannot see at all in daylight.
They are scared of the Sun.
check.why: In India the noon sun is fierce. Moving about in that heat makes an animal lose water and tire quickly. Dawn and dusk are cooler, and there is still a little light to see by. Picking 'cannot see in daylight' is true only for a few animals. Most dawn-and-dusk animals see well in the day.

experiments.title: Busy Times: when do birds visit a water bowl?
experiments.question: At which time of day do the most birds visit a bowl of water on our balcony or window?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the most birds come in the morning, at noon, or in the evening? Write your guess, and why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep everything the same except the time of day. Use the same bowl, in the same place, with fresh water each time. Watch for exactly 10 minutes, sitting in the same spot. Watch on 3 days, because one day might be odd, for example if it rains.

materials.item: a shallow steel or clay bowl, about as wide as a dinner plate
fresh water
a clock or phone timer
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Put the bowl where you can watch from inside, behind a window or a curtain. Do not lean over balcony railings.

schedule.what: Put out the bowl. Guess the busiest time. Watch at 7 am, 12 pm and 5 pm, 10 minutes each time, making tally marks.
Watch again at the same three times. Make tally marks.
Watch at the same three times. Add up the visits. Draw a bar chart and say what you found.

experiments.record: For each 10-minute watch, draw one tally line every time a bird lands at the bowl. Add up each time of day over the 3 days. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for morning, one for noon and one for evening.
experiments.context: This is the Busy Times test. You put a bowl of water outside and count how many birds come to it in 10 minutes, at three different times of day, for three days.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: bird visits to a water bowl over 3 days
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A shallow clay bowl of water on a balcony ledge, with a child behind a window curtain holding a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Put a bowl of water where you can see it from inside.

setup.art: A clock showing 7 o'clock and a myna and a bulbul at the water bowl, with tally marks on a notebook page.
setup.caption: 2. Watch for 10 minutes. Draw one line for each bird that lands.

setup.art: The same notebook with three columns of tally marks labelled with a rising sun, a high sun and a setting sun.
setup.caption: 3. Do it at 7 am, 12 pm and 5 pm, for 3 days.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bowl with fresh water. 2. Put it on a balcony ledge or windowsill, out of reach of cats. 3. Show your child the results table.
flow.say: Birds need water, especially in the hot months. We're going to find out when they come to drink. First, what's your guess? Morning, noon or evening?
flow.kid: Put out a bowl of water for birds. Guess when most birds will come. Morning, noon or evening?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Busy Times test. You put out a bowl of water, then guess when most birds will come to it.
flow.parent: Keep the bowl in the same place for all 3 days. Birds can take a day or two to find a new water bowl, so the first day may be quiet. That is normal. If no bird has come to the bowl by day 2, count instead every bird you see from the same window in 10 minutes. Crows and pigeons live in almost every Indian town, so you will still have numbers to compare.

check.q: Why do we watch at the same spot and for the same 10 minutes each time?
options: So the test is fair. Only the time of day changes.
Because 10 is a lucky number.
So we do not get bored.
check.why: If we watched for 20 minutes in the morning but only 5 at noon, we would count more birds in the morning just because we watched longer. Keeping everything else the same means only the time of day can make the difference. Picking 'lucky number' means not yet seeing why a test must be fair.

flow.do: At 7 am, sit still behind the window for 10 minutes. Make one tally line each time a bird lands at the bowl.
flow.say: Sit very still. Every time a bird lands at the bowl, draw one line. If the same bird comes back, draw another line, because that is another visit.
flow.kid: Sit still and watch the bowl for 10 minutes. Draw one line for each bird that lands.
flow.context: This is the watching step of the Busy Times test, where you count bird visits to a water bowl.
flow.parent: Common visitors are crows, mynas, bulbuls, pigeons, sparrows, sunbirds and squirrels. Count only birds if you can, but note squirrels too. Ask your child to say the kind of bird if they know it.

flow.do: Repeat at 12 pm and at 5 pm. Do the same on days 2 and 3.
flow.say: Same place, same 10 minutes, now at noon. Do you think more birds will come, or fewer?
flow.kid: Now watch at noon, and again at 5 pm. Same place. Same 10 minutes.
flow.context: This step of the Busy Times test repeats the 10-minute watch at noon and in the evening, on three days.
flow.wait: Do this at 7 am, 12 pm and 5 pm on days 2 and 3.

flow.do: On day 3, add the tally marks for each time of day. Draw a bar chart with three bars.
flow.say: Let's add up. How many visits in the morning, over all three days? At noon? In the evening? Now draw one bar for each.
flow.kid: Add up your lines for morning, noon and evening. Draw one bar for each time.
flow.context: This step of the Busy Times test is where you add up your bird counts and draw a bar chart.

check.q: In the made-up results, morning had 14 visits, noon 3, and evening 11. What do they show?
options: Birds drink most in the cool morning and evening, and rest at noon.
Birds never drink water at noon.
Birds like the bowl less every day.
check.why: Most visits came in the cool hours, and very few at noon. Like many Indian animals, birds rest in the shade when it is hottest. Picking 'never drink at noon' goes further than the evidence, because 3 birds did come. Picking 'less every day' mixes up time of day with which day it was.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things, the way scientists report a result. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Busy Times test. You say your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: birds come to drink mostly in the morning and evening. What I saw: 14 visits in the mornings, 11 in the evenings, but only 3 at noon. Why: noon is very hot, so birds rest in the shade and save energy.

experiments.title: Cool Home Test: is a burrow cooler than open ground?
experiments.question: On a hot day, is it cooler inside a hole in the ground than on the open ground in the sun?
experiments.predict: Guess the order before you measure. Which will be hottest: soil in the sun, soil in the shade, or inside a hole in the soil? Which will be coolest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same thermometer for every place. Leave it for the same 5 minutes in each place before reading it. Measure all three places within the same half hour, around noon, so the Sun is the same.

materials.item: a thermometer, such as a digital kitchen probe or a room thermometer
a small trowel or a big spoon
soil in the sun and soil in the shade: the two biggest flower pots you have work, one on a sunny balcony and one in the shade, or a garden bed if you have one
a clock or phone timer

experiments.safety: Do this with a grown-up. Wear a cap, drink water and do not stay in the noon sun for long. Before you dig, look carefully for ants, scorpions and snakes, and dig somewhere else if you see any.

schedule.what: Guess the order. Measure the temperature in the sun, in the shade and inside a hole. Compare.

experiments.record: Write the three temperatures in the table. Put a star next to the coolest place.
experiments.context: This is the Cool Home Test. You measure how hot it is on open ground in the sun, in the shade, and inside a little hole in the soil, like an animal's burrow.

setup.art: A thermometer lying on bare soil in bright sunshine, with a phone timer showing 5 minutes.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the thermometer on soil in the sun for 5 minutes. Read it.

setup.art: The same thermometer lying on the soil of a flower pot in the shade.
setup.caption: 2. Move it to soil in the shade for 5 minutes. Read it.

setup.art: A small hole dug in soil, about a hand deep, with the thermometer pushed inside and the opening loosely covered with a leaf.
setup.caption: 3. Put it inside a small hole for 5 minutes. Read it.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess the order, hottest to coolest.
flow.say: Many animals hide underground in the hot part of the day. Rats, crabs and many insects do. Let's guess first. Which place will be hottest? Why?
flow.kid: Guess. Which is hottest: sun, shade, or inside a hole? Which is coolest?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cool Home Test. You guess which place will be coolest for an animal on a hot day.
flow.parent: No thermometer? Use the back of your hand instead. Touch the top of the sunny soil, then the soil at the bottom of the hole. The difference is easy to feel. Write 'hot', 'warm' or 'cool' in the table instead of numbers.

flow.do: Lay the thermometer on bare soil in full sun. Wait 5 minutes. Read it and write it down.
flow.say: Let's put the thermometer on the open ground first. We wait 5 minutes, so it has time to warm up properly.
flow.kid: Put the thermometer on the soil in the sun. Wait 5 minutes. Read the number.
flow.context: This step of the Cool Home Test measures the open ground in the sun.
flow.parent: On a hot Indian day, soil in the sun can feel too hot to touch, and the thermometer may read over 40 °C. On a cool day the differences are smaller, but still there.

flow.do: Move the thermometer to soil in the shade. Wait 5 minutes. Read it.
flow.say: Now the shade. Same thermometer, same 5 minutes.
flow.kid: Now put it on soil in the shade. Wait 5 minutes. Read the number.
flow.context: This step of the Cool Home Test measures the ground in the shade.

flow.do: In the sunny pot or soil, dig a small hole about as deep as your hand is long. Push the thermometer inside. Cover the opening loosely with a leaf. Wait 5 minutes, then read it.
flow.say: This hole is like a little burrow. Let's see how warm it is inside.
flow.kid: Dig a small hole, a hand deep. Put the thermometer in. Wait 5 minutes. Read it.
flow.context: This step of the Cool Home Test measures the temperature inside a small hole, like an animal's burrow.

check.q: The open sun was 44 °C, the shade 35 °C, and inside the hole 30 °C. Why was the hole coolest?
options: The Sun's heat warms the top of the soil first, and soil is slow to let heat through.
There is ice under the ground.
The thermometer was broken.
check.why: The Sun heats the surface. Soil passes heat down very slowly, so a little way underground stays cool in the day. That is why many animals hide in burrows at noon. Picking 'ice' means guessing without evidence. Picking 'broken' is worth checking, but the same thermometer gave sensible readings in the other two places.

flow.do: Fill in the hole. Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Let's fill the hole in, so no one trips. Now, like a scientist: what do you think, what did you see, and why?
flow.kid: Fill the hole in. Then say: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Cool Home Test. You tidy up, then say your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: a burrow keeps an animal cool on a hot day. What I saw: the hole was 30 °C, but the open ground was 44 °C. Why: the Sun heats the top of the ground, and the heat moves down slowly.

experiments.title: Ant Trail Test: how do ants keep to the same path?
experiments.question: Ants walk to food along the same path, one behind another. If we rub away a short piece of the path, can the ants still find their way?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. When you rub your finger across the ant trail, what will the ants do? Will they walk straight on, stop, or go round? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, count the ants crossing the same spot for the same 1 minute each time. First hold your finger just above the trail without touching it. If the ants carry on, we know our hand and its shadow do not stop them. Then rub the floor with the same finger. Now the only new thing is touching the trail.
results_table: Ants crossing the spot in 1 minute

materials.item: a pinch of sugar, or a drop of honey
a small square of paper to put the sugar on
a clock or phone timer
a pencil and the results table
a clean dry tissue, for the extra try

experiments.safety: Use small black or brown house ants. Do not use red ants, big or small, because they bite or sting. Wash your hands after rubbing the floor.

schedule.what: About an hour before, put out the sugar where you have seen ants. When a trail has formed, count the ants, test the trail and say what you found.

experiments.record: Write the number of ants that crossed the spot in 1 minute: before, with a hand above, just after rubbing, and 3 minutes after rubbing. Next to each number, write what the ants did.
experiments.context: This is the Ant Trail Test. You put out a pinch of sugar, wait for a line of ants to walk to it, and then rub away a short piece of their path to see what they do.

setup.art: A pinch of sugar on a small square of paper on a kitchen floor tile, with a thin line of small black ants walking to it from a gap under a cupboard.
setup.caption: 1. Put a pinch of sugar where ants come. Wait for a trail.

setup.art: A child's finger held just above the ant trail, not touching, with the ants walking on underneath.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a finger just above the trail. Count the ants for 1 minute.

setup.art: A child's finger rubbing a short strip across the ant trail, and ants stopping and turning in circles at the strip.
setup.caption: 3. Rub a short strip across the trail. Watch what the ants do.

flow.do: 1. About an hour before, put a pinch of sugar on a square of paper where you have seen ants. 2. Wait until a line of ants walks to it. 3. Show your child the trail.
flow.say: Look, the ants walk in a line, one behind another. How do you think they all know the way to the sugar?
flow.kid: Look at the line of ants. How do they all know the way?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ant Trail Test. You set out sugar and wait for a line of ants.
flow.parent: Ants usually find sugar within an hour, often much sooner, but only where ants already come. So first look for ants: on the kitchen floor, along counter edges, on window sills, the balcony or the stairs. Ants are slower in cold weather, so try on a warm afternoon. If no ants come, leave the sugar out overnight and look in the morning. You can also try the stairs or the bottom of an outside wall of your building. Fast, long-legged ants that run about wildly follow trails loosely. Small black or brown ants walking in a neat line work best.

flow.do: Choose one spot where the ants walk in a neat, thin line, at least a hand away from the sugar. Count the ants that walk past it in 1 minute. Write the number.
flow.say: Let's count how many ants walk past this spot in one minute. Then we will know what the trail is like before we change anything.
flow.kid: Pick one spot on the trail. Count the ants that pass it in 1 minute.
flow.context: This step of the Ant Trail Test counts the ants on the trail before anything is changed.

ask.q: Now guess. What will the ants do if you rub your finger across their path? Why do you think so?
good: They will get lost, because they follow something on the floor.
They will walk on, because they can see the other ants.

flow.parent: Wait for a guess and a reason before going on. Any guess is fine. The test will answer it.

flow.do: Hold one finger just above the trail at the spot, without touching the floor, for 10 seconds. Keep it still, and do not breathe on the ants. Then count the ants passing the spot for 1 minute.
flow.say: First I hold my finger just above the trail, without touching. Do the ants stop? Let's count them for one minute.
flow.kid: Hold your finger just above the ants. Do not touch. Count them for 1 minute.
flow.context: This step of the Ant Trail Test checks whether a hand above the trail, and its shadow, change what the ants do.
flow.parent: Usually the ants carry on, with perhaps a short pause. This try shows that our hand alone does not stop them.

flow.do: Rub one finger firmly back and forth across the trail at the spot, three or four times. Make a strip about two fingers wide. Watch the strip from the moment you lift your finger. Count the ants crossing it in the first minute, and again in the third minute.
flow.say: Now I rub my finger across the floor where the ants walk. Watch the strip closely. What do the ants do when they reach it?
flow.kid: Rub your finger across the trail. Watch the ants at that spot. What do they do?
flow.context: This step of the Ant Trail Test is the real test. You rub away a short piece of the ants' path and watch what happens.
flow.parent: Watch closely in the first few seconds, because the pause can be short. Expect the ants to stop at the strip, wave their feelers, turn back or wander in circles. Within a minute or two a few ants cross, and soon the line forms again. If the ants hardly pause, rub harder, make the strip about four fingers wide, and try again. If you have time, try once more with a clean dry tissue instead of your finger. If the ants stop then too, your finger's own smell was not the reason.

check.q: Before rubbing, 12 ants crossed the spot in one minute. With a hand above, 11 crossed. In the first minute after rubbing, only 2 crossed. What is the best explanation?
options: The ants follow something on the floor, and rubbing took it away.
The ants are scared of hands.
The ants were tired.
check.why: A hand above the trail hardly changed anything, so the hand was not the reason. Rubbing the floor did. Ants leave a smell trail made of a chemical called a pheromone. Other ants follow the smell to the food and add their own as they go. Rubbing wiped the smell away, so the ants lost the path until some crossed and laid it again. Picking 'scared of hands' does not fit, because the ants walked on under the hand. Picking 'tired' does not explain why they stopped only at the rubbed strip.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write what they think, what they saw, and why. Then wipe up the sugar.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think the ants did that?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why. Then wipe up the sugar.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Ant Trail Test. You say your claim, your evidence and your reasoning, then tidy up.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: ants find their way by following a smell on the floor. What I saw: the ants walked on when my hand was above them, but stopped and wandered where I rubbed the floor. After a few minutes the line came back. Why: rubbing wiped away their smell trail, and new ants laid it again. This is how a whole line of ants keeps to one path. Afterwards, wipe up the sugar and wipe the floor with a damp cloth, so the ants stop coming to that spot.

activities.title: Ten-Minute Window Watch

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a clock or phone timer

activities.safety: Watch from inside, or from a safe step outside. Do not lean out of windows.

schedule.what: Watch from one window or door for 10 minutes. Write every animal and what it does.

activities.record: Make two columns: WHAT I SAW and WHAT IT WAS DOING. Then circle the animal you want to watch for a whole week.
activities.context: This is a short watching activity. You sit at one window or door for 10 minutes and write down every animal you see or hear, and what each one is doing.

setup.art: A child sitting very still on a stool by an open window, a notebook on her knee and a phone timer beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still at a window for 10 minutes.

setup.art: A view from the window with small arrows pointing to a crow on a wire, ants on the wall, a pigeon on a ledge and a squirrel on a tree.
setup.caption: 2. Look high, low, near and far. Listen too.

setup.art: A notebook page with two columns and little drawings: a crow calling, ants carrying crumbs, a pigeon sitting.
setup.caption: 3. Write what you saw and what it was doing.

flow.do: Choose a window or a door with a view of a tree, a wall or a street. Set a timer for 10 minutes.
flow.say: We're going to be naturalists. A naturalist is someone who studies animals by watching them quietly. For 10 minutes, we'll write down every animal we see or hear.
flow.kid: You are a naturalist now. Sit still for 10 minutes. Write every animal you see or hear.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ten-Minute Window Watch. You get ready to watch animals from a window.

flow.do: Watch together, quietly. Help your child look high (sky, wires, roof), low (ground, walls, corners) and listen.
flow.say: Look up at the sky and the wires. Now look down at the walls and the ground. Now close your eyes and just listen. What can you hear?
flow.kid: Look up. Look down. Look at the corners. Then close your eyes and listen.
flow.context: This is the watching step of the Ten-Minute Window Watch.
flow.parent: Most children find 2 or 3 animals in the first minute and many more by the end. Count tiny ones too, like ants, flies, spiders and mosquitoes. Count sounds you hear, such as a koel or a dog.

flow.do: Read the list together. Ask what each animal was doing. Circle one animal to watch for a week.
flow.say: Look how many we found. Which one was doing the most interesting thing? Let's choose one animal to watch all week.
flow.kid: Read your list. Which animal was most interesting? Circle it. You will watch it all week.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Ten-Minute Window Watch. You look at your list and choose an animal to watch for a week.

check.q: You saw a crow sitting on a wire for one minute. What can you say for sure?
options: The crow always sits on that wire.
The crow sat on the wire this time.
The crow lives on the wire.
check.why: One watch tells you what happened once. To know what an animal usually does, you need to watch it many times. That is why we watch for a week. Picking 'always sits there' is a guess about a habit made from one look. Picking 'lives on the wire' mixes up sitting somewhere with living there.

activities.title: Animal Homes Walk and Map

materials.item: a large sheet of paper and crayons
a magnifying glass, if you have one
binoculars, if you have them

activities.safety: Go with a grown-up. Look but do not touch nests, holes, webs or hives. Do not put your hand into any hole, because snakes and scorpions may hide there. Stay away from bee hives.

schedule.what: Walk around your building, street or park. Find animal homes. Draw them on a map.

activities.record: Draw a map of where you walked. Mark every animal home you found with a small picture. Write who you think lives there.
activities.context: This is a walk to find animal homes near your house: nests, holes, webs, hives and anthills. Then you draw them on a map of your area.

setup.art: A parent and child walking along a lane, the child pointing up at a nest in a tree.
setup.caption: 1. Walk slowly around your area. Look up, down and into corners.

setup.art: Close-ups of a spider web in a gate, an anthill by a wall and a hole in a tree trunk.
setup.caption: 2. Find homes: nests, webs, holes, hives and anthills.

setup.art: A hand-drawn map of a street with small pictures of a nest, a web, a hive and an anthill in the right places.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a map. Mark each home where you found it.

flow.do: Explain the walk. Agree the safety rules together.
flow.say: We're going on a hunt for animal homes. Nests, holes, webs, hives and anthills. The rule is: we look, we never touch, and we never put a hand in a hole.
flow.kid: Let's hunt for animal homes. Look, but never touch. Never put your hand into a hole.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Animal Homes Walk. You agree the rules before you look for animal homes.

flow.do: Walk slowly for about 20 minutes. Stop at every home you find. Let your child sketch it quickly.
flow.say: Look up into the trees and under the roof edges. Look along walls for little holes and lines of ants. Look in corners for webs.
flow.kid: Look up in the trees. Look at the walls and corners. Draw each home you find.
flow.context: This is the walking step of the Animal Homes Walk, where you search for animal homes.
flow.parent: Common finds: crow and pigeon nests, sparrow holes in walls, webs in gates and plants, anthills at the base of walls, termite trails of mud on tree trunks, holes in tree trunks, and in some cities giant rock bee hives under water tanks.

check.q: You find a neat round hole in an old tree trunk, high up. Who might use it?
options: A parakeet, an owl or a barbet, as a nest
A cow, to sleep in
Nobody. Holes are just empty.
check.why: Holes in old trees are valuable homes. Barbets and woodpeckers dig them. Later, parakeets, owls, mynas and squirrels move in. Picking 'cow' ignores the size. Picking 'nobody' is a common mistake, because an empty-looking hole may be someone's home.

flow.do: At home, draw a map of the walk on the big sheet. Mark each home with a little picture.
flow.say: Let's draw our walk as a map. Where was the anthill? Where was the nest? Who do you think lives in each one?
flow.kid: Draw a map of your walk. Draw each home where you found it. Write who lives there.
flow.context: This is the map step of the Animal Homes Walk. You draw your area and mark the animal homes you found.
flow.think: Which part of your area had the most homes? Why do you think so?

activities.title: Animal Signs Bingo

materials.item: a printed bingo card with 9 squares
a pencil

activities.safety: Go with a grown-up. Do not touch droppings, dead animals or shed snake skins with bare hands.

schedule.what: Walk outside and tick off animal signs on your bingo card.

activities.record: Tick each square when you find the sign. Write where you found it.
activities.context: This is a bingo game played on a walk. Instead of finding animals, you find signs that animals have been there, like feathers, footprints and chewed leaves.

setup.art: A bingo card with 9 picture squares: a feather, a footprint, a chewed leaf, a web, a line of ants, bird droppings, a nest, a hole and a musical note for a call.
setup.caption: 1. Take your bingo card on a walk.

setup.art: A child crouching to look at a chewed leaf with holes in it, a pencil in her hand.
setup.caption: 2. Look for signs that an animal has been there.

setup.art: A bingo card with three ticks in a row and a child cheering.
setup.caption: 3. Three in a row is bingo. Can you fill the card?

flow.do: Show the bingo card. Explain that we are looking for signs, not animals.
flow.say: Animals are often hiding. But they leave clues. A feather, a footprint, a chewed leaf. Let's find nine clues.
flow.kid: Animals leave clues. Find nine clues on your bingo card.
flow.context: This is the first step of Animal Signs Bingo. You learn that animals leave signs you can find.

flow.do: Walk and tick squares. At each find, ask who left it.
flow.say: A chewed leaf! Who do you think ate it? A caterpillar? A snail? A goat?
flow.kid: Find a clue. Tick it. Say who left it.
flow.context: This is the walking step of Animal Signs Bingo.

check.q: You see white splashes under one branch of a tree, every day. What might it mean?
options: Birds roost or sit on that branch often.
Someone spilled paint there.
The tree is ill.
check.why: Bird droppings in one place every day mean birds sit or sleep above it again and again. That is a habit, and the droppings are the evidence. Picking 'paint' is possible once, but not every day. Picking 'ill tree' mixes up a sign of animals with a sign of the plant.

flow.do: Count the ticks. Ask which sign told the most.
flow.say: Which clue told us the most about an animal's habits?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Which clue was the best?
flow.context: This is the last step of Animal Signs Bingo.

activities.title: Build a Nest with a Beak

materials.item: a handful of broom sticks broken short, cotton thread, wool scraps, thin strips of newspaper and a few dry leaves
a clothes peg or a pair of kitchen tongs, to be the beak
a small bowl
a marble, a small lemon or a small ball, as the egg

activities.safety: Use clean materials. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Try to build a nest using only a peg as a beak. Test it with an egg.

activities.record: Draw your nest. Write how many minutes it took, and whether the egg stayed in.
activities.context: This activity lets you feel how hard it is to be a bird building a nest. You can only use a clothes peg, like a beak, to carry and weave twigs and grass.

setup.art: A pile of short broom sticks, thread, wool, newspaper strips and dry leaves on newspaper, with a clothes peg beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Collect sticks, thread, wool and paper strips. The peg is your beak.

setup.art: A child's hand holding a clothes peg, picking up a single short stick and placing it in a small bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Carry one piece at a time with the peg. Build in a bowl.

setup.art: A rough nest of twigs and grass with a pebble egg sitting in it, being tipped gently.
setup.caption: 3. Put an egg in. Tip the nest gently. Does it hold?

flow.do: Lay out the materials. Give your child the clothes peg.
flow.say: Birds have no hands. They build their whole nest with their beak, one piece at a time. Today, the peg is your beak.
flow.kid: Birds build with only a beak. The peg is your beak. No hands allowed!
flow.context: This is the first step of Build a Nest with a Beak. You get ready to build like a bird.

flow.do: Let your child build for 15 minutes, carrying one piece at a time with the peg.
flow.say: One piece at a time. Which pieces hold together best? Where would you put the soft wool?
flow.kid: Carry one piece at a time with the peg. Put the soft bits inside.
flow.context: This is the building step of Build a Nest with a Beak.
flow.parent: Children quickly find that sticks alone fall apart. Thread and paper strips wound around help. Soft wool is best inside. A real bird makes many trips to build one nest, carrying one piece each time.

flow.do: Put the egg in. Tip the bowl gently.
flow.say: Let's test it. Put the egg in, and tip the nest a little, like a branch in the wind.
flow.kid: Put your egg in. Tip the nest gently. Does the egg stay in?
flow.context: This is the testing step of Build a Nest with a Beak.

check.q: Why do city crows often use wire in their nests?
options: Wire is easy to find in cities, and it bends and holds its shape.
Crows prefer metal to wood.
Wire keeps the eggs warm.
check.why: Birds build with what they find nearby. In cities there is plenty of wire, and it bends round a branch and stays put. Picking 'prefer metal' goes too far. Crows in villages use twigs. Picking 'keeps eggs warm' is not right, because wire does not keep heat in. Soft lining does that.

flow.do: Ask what was hardest.
flow.say: What was the hardest part? Do you think a bird gets better with practice?
flow.kid: What was hardest? Would you get better with practice?
flow.context: This is the last step of Build a Nest with a Beak.
flow.think: Young weaver birds weave messy nests at first and better ones later. What does that tell you?

activities.title: Town, Village, Forest

materials.item: a big sheet of paper folded into three parts
24 small animal picture cards, drawn or printed

schedule.what: Sort animal cards into town, village and forest. Find the ones that belong in more than one.

activities.record: Stick or draw each animal in its place. Draw animals that live in two or three places on the fold lines.
activities.context: This is a sorting activity. You decide which animals live in Indian towns, villages and forests, and you find out that many live in more than one place.

setup.art: A sheet folded into three panels with drawings of buildings, huts with fields, and tall trees at the top of each panel.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a sheet into three: town, village and forest.

setup.art: A child placing a card of a crow on the town panel, with a cow card and a tiger card waiting.
setup.caption: 2. Put each animal card where it lives.

setup.art: Cards of a monkey, a leopard and a peacock lying across the fold lines between panels.
setup.caption: 3. Some animals live in two places. Put them on the folds.

flow.do: Fold the sheet into three. Label the parts Town, Village and Forest.
flow.say: India's animals live in towns, villages and forests. Let's sort them out. But watch carefully, because some may surprise you.
flow.kid: Fold your paper into three: town, village, forest. Get your animal cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Town, Village, Forest, a sorting activity about where Indian animals live.

flow.do: Sort the 24 cards together. Start with crow, pigeon, myna, palm squirrel, street dog, house gecko, rat and fruit bat. Then do cow, buffalo, goat, hen, peacock, cattle egret, frog and rat snake. Last, do weaver bird, tiger, elephant, sloth bear, great hornbill, langur, rhesus macaque and leopard.
flow.say: Where does this one live? Could it live in more than one place?
flow.kid: Put each card where the animal lives. Can any live in two places?
flow.context: This is the sorting step of Town, Village, Forest.
flow.parent: Many cards can go on a fold. Macaques and langurs live in forests and in towns. Peacocks live in villages and forests. Leopards live in forests, near villages, and at the edge of Mumbai. Fruit bats roost in big trees in towns and villages. There is no single right answer, as long as the reason is good.

check.q: Where do leopards live in India?
options: Only in deep forests far from people
In forests, and also near villages and at the edge of cities like Mumbai
Only in zoos
check.why: Leopards live in many places, including farmland and the edges of towns. Sanjay Gandhi National Park, inside Mumbai, has leopards that walk past homes at night. Picking 'only deep forests' is the most common belief, but the evidence shows otherwise.

flow.do: Look at the folds. Ask why those animals do well in more than one place.
flow.say: Look at the animals on the folds. What do they have in common?
flow.kid: Look at the animals on the folds. Why can they live in many places?
flow.context: This is the last step of Town, Village, Forest.

ask.q: Why can crows and macaques live almost anywhere?
good: They eat many kinds of food.
They are clever and not too shy of people.

activities.title: Sound Map

materials.item: a sheet of paper with an X in the middle for you
a pencil

activities.safety: Sit somewhere safe, away from traffic.

schedule.what: Sit still for 5 minutes and mark every animal sound on a map around you.

activities.record: Mark each animal sound where it came from, with a small drawing or a letter.
activities.context: This is a listening activity. You sit very still with your eyes closed and mark every animal sound you hear on a map, with yourself in the middle.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a small X in the middle and the word ME, and a child sitting cross-legged on a terrace.
setup.caption: 1. Draw an X in the middle of the paper. That is you.

setup.art: The child with eyes closed, cupping one ear, with sound waves coming from a tree and a rooftop.
setup.caption: 2. Close your eyes and listen for 5 minutes.

setup.art: The same paper with small drawings around the X: a crow up and to the left, a dog down and to the right, a koel far away at the top.
setup.caption: 3. Mark each sound in the direction it came from.

flow.do: Sit outside or by an open window. Draw an X in the middle of the paper.
flow.say: This X is you. We'll close our eyes and listen. Every time we hear an animal, we'll mark it on the paper, in the direction it came from.
flow.kid: The X is you. Close your eyes. Listen for animals.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sound Map. You get ready to listen for animals around you.

flow.do: Listen in silence for 5 minutes. Open eyes briefly to mark each sound.
flow.say: Shh. Near or far? Up or down? Left or right?
flow.kid: Listen. Is the sound near or far? Mark it on your map.
flow.context: This is the listening step of the Sound Map.
flow.parent: Common sounds: crows, koels, mynas, pigeons cooing, dogs barking, squirrels chattering, crickets and frogs in the evening. A Sound Map at dawn and another at dusk shows how animal habits change through the day.

flow.do: Look at the map together.
flow.say: How many animals did we hear but never see? Which way were most of them?
flow.kid: How many animals did you hear? How many did you see?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Sound Map.
flow.think: Do the sounds change at night? Try a Sound Map after dark, with a grown-up.

projects.title: My Animal Week

materials.item: a notebook to be your animal diary
a pencil and crayons
a clock or phone
binoculars, if you have them

projects.safety: Watch from a distance. Never touch the animal, its nest or its young. If you watch a street dog, a cow or monkeys, a grown-up must be with you and you keep well away.

schedule.what: Choose one animal you can find every day. Make the diary table. Watch for 10 minutes and write down the times.
Watch at the same time and place. Add one new detail, such as what it eats or where it goes.
Watch at a different time of day. Is the animal doing something different?
Watch at the first time again. Draw your animal from life.
Watch and count one behaviour with tally marks, such as how many times it eats or calls.
Watch at dusk or dawn, with a grown-up. Where does it go to rest?
Read the whole diary. Find patterns. Draw a timeline of your animal's day. Say your claim, evidence and reasoning.

projects.record: Each day write the date, the time, the weather and what the animal did. On day 7, draw a timeline from morning to night with what your animal does at each time.
projects.context: In this 7-day project you watch one animal near your home, such as a crow, a pigeon, a squirrel, an ant trail or a gecko, for about 10 minutes every day. At the end you find its habits.

setup.art: A child choosing between pictures of a crow, a pigeon, a squirrel, an ant trail and a gecko, pointing at the squirrel.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one animal you can find every day.

setup.art: An open diary with a table: date, time, weather, what it did, and a small sketch of a squirrel on a wall.
setup.caption: 2. Watch for 10 minutes each day. Write the time and what it did.

setup.art: A drawn timeline from sunrise to night, with a squirrel shown waking, eating, resting in shade, eating again and going to its nest.
setup.caption: 3. On day 7, draw your animal's day as a timeline.

flow.do: Help your child choose one animal they can find every day near home. Make the diary table: Date, Time, Weather, What it did.
flow.say: Real naturalists watch one animal for a long time. That's how they find its habits. Which animal can we find every single day?
flow.kid: Choose one animal you can find every day. It is your animal for the week.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Animal Week, a 7-day project where you watch one animal and find its habits.
flow.parent: Easy choices: a crow or pigeon pair on a ledge or tree, palm squirrels, an ant trail in the kitchen, a house gecko near a tube light at night, a spider in its web, or a cow in the lane. An ant trail or a spider is good if you live high up.

flow.do: Watch for 10 minutes. Write the time and every action, as facts.
flow.say: Write only what you see. 'The squirrel ran up the wall at 7:15' is a fact. 'The squirrel was happy' is a guess. Facts first.
flow.kid: Watch for 10 minutes. Write the time and what it did. Only write what you see.
flow.context: This is the first day's watch of My Animal Week.

check.q: Which of these is a fact you saw, not a guess?
options: The pigeon was sad.
The pigeon sat on the ledge from 7:10 to 7:25 with its feathers puffed up.
The pigeon is the oldest pigeon in the city.
check.why: A fact is something you saw or measured, with the time. 'Sad' is a guess about a feeling you cannot see. 'Oldest' is a guess you have no way to check. Puffed feathers and the time are things anyone else could also see.

flow.do: Days 2 to 6: watch for 10 minutes each day, following the schedule.
flow.say: Today, watch at a different time. Is your animal doing the same thing as before, or something new?
flow.kid: Watch your animal again today. Is it doing the same thing, or something new?
flow.context: This step of My Animal Week covers the daily watches on days 2 to 6.
flow.wait: Come back to this each day from day 2 to day 6, for about 10 minutes.
flow.parent: On day 6, watch at dawn or dusk with your child. Many animals go to a roost, a nest or a hiding place then. Children are often amazed to see where their animal sleeps.

flow.do: Day 7: read the diary together. Look for things that happened again and again. Draw a timeline of the animal's day.
flow.say: Let's read the whole week. What did your animal do more than once? At what times? Now let's draw its day, from morning to night.
flow.kid: Read your whole diary. What happened again and again? Draw your animal's day.
flow.context: This is the day 7 step of My Animal Week, where you look for patterns in your diary.

check.q: Your ants were busy on the sugar tin every evening, but you never saw them there in the morning. What is the best claim?
options: Ants hate mornings.
In my kitchen, the ants come to the sugar mostly in the evening.
All ants in the world eat only in the evening.
check.why: A good claim says what you found, where you found it, and no more. You watched one ant trail in one kitchen. Picking 'all ants in the world' goes far beyond your evidence. Picking 'hate mornings' is a guess about a feeling. Maybe the kitchen is busy with people in the morning, so the ants keep away.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning about one habit.
flow.say: Tell me like a scientist. What is one habit of your animal? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it does that?
flow.kid: Say one habit of your animal. Say what you saw. Say why you think it does that.
flow.context: This is the last step of My Animal Week. You share one habit with your claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: our squirrels rest in the afternoon. What I saw: on 5 days, they were running about at 7 am, but at 2 pm they lay flat on the shady wall. Why: it is very hot at 2 pm, and lying flat on cool stone helps them cool down.

challenges.title: Design a Sparrow Home
challenges.problem: House sparrows nest in holes in walls and roofs. Many new buildings have smooth walls with no holes. Design and make a nest box that a pair of sparrows could use.
constraints: The entrance hole should be about 3 cm wide, about one and a half times as wide as a one-rupee coin. Bigger holes let in crows and mynas.
The box must be out of reach of cats, and in shade, at least as high as a door.
No paint or glue inside the box, because chicks could swallow it.
The box must keep out rain.
materials: a strong cardboard box, such as a shoebox, or a wooden box
scissors, used by a grown-up for the hole
string or wire to hang it
dry grass for a little lining, optional
an old plastic sheet or a tile for a roof
general: Make a box about 15 cm tall and 12 cm wide, with a 3 cm round hole near the top of the front.
Put a slanting roof on top so rain runs off.
Make a few small holes in the bottom so any water drains out.
Hang it under a balcony roof or a shady wall, facing away from strong afternoon sun.
creative: Some families make sparrow boxes from old wooden crates, or from clay pots sold for this.
Plant a small bush or a pot of flowering plants nearby. Insects come to the plants, and sparrow chicks eat insects.
Put a shallow bowl of water near the box in summer.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own sparrow home. Draw it, make it, and hang it with a grown-up. Then watch it every day for a month. Write down any bird that comes.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a nest box for house sparrows, birds that live near people and need small holes to nest in.

setup.art: A child drawing a design for a box with a small round hole and a slanting roof on paper.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your sparrow home first.

setup.art: A parent cutting a round hole in a cardboard box, with a one-rupee coin beside it to compare the size.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up cuts a hole about 3 cm wide.

setup.art: A finished nest box with a tile roof hanging under a shady balcony roof, a sparrow looking at the hole.
setup.caption: 3. Hang it high and in the shade. Watch who comes.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints.
flow.say: Sparrows used to nest in the holes of old houses. New buildings are smooth, with no holes. Can we design a home for them?
flow.kid: Sparrows need small holes to nest in. Can you design one?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Design a Sparrow Home challenge.

flow.do: Draw a design. Check it against each constraint.
flow.say: Why do you think the hole must be small?
flow.kid: Draw your sparrow home. Check: small hole, shade, no paint inside, rain roof.
flow.context: This is the design step of the Sparrow Home challenge.

check.q: Why should a sparrow box have a small hole, about 3 cm wide?
options: So bigger birds like crows and mynas cannot get in and take the eggs
So the sparrows feel squeezed
So the box looks nicer
check.why: A small hole lets a sparrow in but keeps out bigger birds that might take the eggs or the box. Picking 'looks nicer' means thinking about us, not the bird. A good design starts with what the animal needs.

flow.do: Make the box. A grown-up cuts the hole. Hang it in shade, high up.
flow.say: Let's build it. I'll cut the hole. You make the roof. Then we'll hang it high, in the shade.

challenges.title: Share the Space
challenges.problem: A pair of pigeons keeps trying to nest on the outdoor box of your air conditioner, and the family is unhappy about the mess. Plan a way to share your building with the pigeons that does not harm them.
constraints: You must not harm any bird, egg or chick.
If there are already eggs or chicks, you must wait until the chicks have flown before changing anything.
Your plan must work for both the family and the birds.
materials: paper and pencil to draw a plan
pictures of your building, drawn or photographed
general: Before any eggs are laid, cover the spot with bird netting, so the pigeons choose somewhere else.
Clean the ledge often and keep it clear. Pigeons choose quiet spots where nobody disturbs them.
Give the birds another safe place, such as a ledge you do not mind them using.
creative: Make a 'pigeon diary' first. Find out what times they come, like Tara did in the story. Maybe there is a pattern you can use.
Talk to neighbours and make a building plan, so the birds are not pushed from one flat to the next.
Draw a poster for your building about watching kindly.
challenges.your_turn: Now think of an animal that shares your home or street, such as ants, a gecko, monkeys or a dog. Draw a plan for how you and that animal can share the space safely.
challenges.context: This is a thinking challenge. You plan how people and animals that nest in buildings can share the space without anyone being harmed.

check.q: You find two pigeon eggs on the AC box. What should you do?
options: Throw the nest away at once.
Leave it until the chicks fly, then cover the spot before the next nesting.
Move the eggs to the ground.
check.why: Once there are eggs, the kind thing is to wait. Pigeon chicks fly about a month after hatching. Then you clean up and cover the spot. Throwing the nest away kills the chicks. Moving eggs to the ground leaves them cold and in danger, because the parents may not find them.

items.p: What is a habit?
opts: Something an animal does only once
Something an animal does again and again, often at the same time
The place where an animal lives
items.why: A habit is a repeated behaviour, like crows calling at first light every day. Picking 'only once' is the opposite. Picking 'place where it lives' mixes up habit with habitat or home.

items.p: Which animal is nocturnal, active at night?
items.why: Fruit bats rest in trees in the day and fly out at dusk to find fruit. Squirrels, crows and butterflies are busy in the day. Picking one of them usually means guessing from animals we see most.

items.p: A home that a bird builds for its eggs and chicks is called a ____.
items.why: A nest is built to lay eggs and raise young. Most birds leave it once the chicks fly.

items.p: A tunnel that an animal digs in the ground to live in is called a ____.
items.why: Rats, porcupines, crabs and many snakes use burrows. Burrows stay cool in the day.

items.p: Match each animal to its home.
items.why: Each animal builds or finds a home that suits it. Bees make wax, weavers weave grass, spiders spin silk, termites pile soil, and owls move into tree holes.

items.p: Sort these animals. Are they busy mostly in the DAY or at NIGHT?
items.why: Owls, geckos and moths are nocturnal. Crows, mynas and honey bees are diurnal, busy in daylight.

items.p: Most birds sleep in their nests every night of the year.
items.why: False. Most birds use a nest only for eggs and chicks. The rest of the year they sleep perched on branches or at a roost.

items.p: Wild animals can live in cities.
items.why: True. Crows, kites, palm squirrels, geckos and even leopards near Mumbai are wild animals that live in or around cities.

items.p: Why do many animals hide in burrows at noon in India?
opts: They are scared of the dark.
Burrows have more food at noon.
items.why: The Sun heats the top of the ground, but a little way down it stays cool. Picking 'scared of the dark' gets it backwards, because burrows are dark. Picking 'more food' is not why. They go there to rest and stay cool.

items.p: Which of these is a domestic animal?
items.why: A cow has been kept and bred by people for thousands of years. A crow, squirrel and leopard are wild, even if they live near us. Picking 'crow' is a common mistake, because crows live so close to us.

items.p: Animals that are most busy at dawn and dusk are called ____.
items.why: Crepuscular means busy in the dim light of dawn and dusk. Many mosquitoes and deer are crepuscular.

items.p: Crows dive at people walking under one tree in May. What is the most likely reason?
opts: They are guarding a nest with eggs or chicks.
items.why: In the nesting months, crows guard their nests and dive at anyone who comes close. Picking 'mad' explains nothing. It is what Murugan thought in the story before Tara watched for a week.

items.p: Name three animals you have seen near your home. For each one, write one habit.
items.a: For example: Crows call loudly at first light. Pigeons sit on the window ledge in the afternoon. Ants walk in a line to the sugar tin in the evening.
items.why: A good answer names a real animal and something it does again and again, with a time or place if possible.

items.p: Why do we watch an animal for a week, not just once?
items.a: One watch only shows what the animal did that one time. Watching many times shows what it usually does, so we can find its habits.
items.why: Habits are patterns. A pattern only appears after many watches.

items.p: Draw one animal home you have seen near your house. Label who lives there and what it is made of.
items.a: Any real home, for example a crow's nest of sticks and wire in a tree, a web in a gate, or an anthill by a wall, with labels.
items.why: Drawing from life makes you look closely at how a home is made.
items.art: An empty box with a small tree outline in the corner.

items.p: In the Busy Times test, why did we watch on 3 different days?
opts: Because one day might be unusual, for example if it rains.
Because birds only drink every third day.
items.why: Repeating on several days means one odd day cannot fool us. Picking 'birds drink every third day' invents a fact. Repeating is about trusting our results.

items.p: In the Cool Home Test, the open ground was 44 °C and inside the hole was 30 °C. How much cooler was the hole?
items.why: 44 take away 30 is 14. So the hole was 14 degrees cooler. Picking 74 means adding instead of taking away. Picking 30 is just the hole's own temperature.

items.p: In the Ant Trail Test, why did we first hold a finger just above the trail, without touching it?
opts: To check that our hand and its shadow were not what stopped the ants
To make the ants walk faster
To count the ants more easily
items.why: If the ants stopped only when we rubbed the floor, and not when a hand was above them, then the rubbing is the reason. This try rules out the hand. Picking 'to feed the ants' misses that a fair test changes one thing at a time.

items.p: A tiger has no fixed home. It rests anywhere inside its large area.
items.why: True. A tiger roams a large area to find enough prey. It does not build a home.

items.p: A koel builds a big nest and raises its own chicks.
items.why: False. A koel lays its egg in a crow's nest, and the crows raise the koel chick.

items.p: Why do rock pigeons nest on window ledges in cities?
opts: Ledges are like the cliff ledges their wild relatives used.
People put food on every ledge.
Ledges are warmer than trees in winter only.
items.why: Wild rock pigeons nest on cliffs. Tall buildings with ledges look like cliffs to them. Picking 'cannot fly high' is wrong. Pigeons fly very well.

items.p: Match each animal to why it lives near people.
pairs: food scraps, and shelter in drains
items.why: Each animal lives near people because people give it something it needs, such as food or shelter.

items.p: Put a house crow's day in order, from morning to night.
items: looks for food in the morning
rests in the shade at noon
flies to the roost tree at sunset
items.why: Crows wake and call at first light, feed in the cooler morning, rest at noon and gather at a roost in the evening.

items.p: A place where many birds or bats rest or sleep together is called a ____.
items.why: Crows, mynas, parakeets and fruit bats gather in big trees to roost.

items.p: Which note is a fact, not a guess?
opts: At 7:15 the squirrel ran up the wall with a twig in its mouth.
The squirrel is the cleverest in town.
items.why: A fact has a time and something anyone could see. Feelings and 'cleverest' are guesses we cannot check by watching.

items.p: Termite mounds near Bengaluru were studied in 2015. What helps the air inside them move?
opts: The walls warming in the day and cooling at night
items.why: Scientists found that the mound's outer walls warm up and cool down faster than its middle, as day turns to night. That moves the air. Picking 'body warmth' is the older idea, which the measurements did not support for these mounds.

items.p: Snakes come to houses mainly to drink milk.
items.why: False. Snakes come to hunt rats, frogs and other animals. Snakes cannot digest milk well.

items.p: Bar-headed geese spend the summer in Central Asia and the winter in India. What is this called?
items.why: Travelling far at the same time each year and coming back is migration. Hibernation is a deep winter sleep, which these geese do not do.

items.p: Pick one animal home. Explain how the animal makes it, and what it is for.
items.a: A baya weaver bird tears long strips of grass and weaves them into a hanging nest with a long tube for a door. It is for laying eggs and raising chicks safe from snakes.
items.why: A good answer says how the home is made and what it is used for.

items.p: In the story The Wire Nest, how did Tara find out why the crows were diving?
items.a: She wrote down the time and the place of every dive for several days. She saw that the dives happened only in the morning and evening, and only under the nest. So the crows were guarding their chicks.
items.why: Tara found a pattern by watching many times and writing it down.

items.p: A fruit fly is kept in total darkness for a week. What happens to its waking and sleeping?
opts: It keeps waking and resting on a cycle of about 24 hours.
It wakes at a random time each day.
items.why: Its body clock keeps running in the dark, on a cycle of about one day. Picking 'sleeps all the time' assumes darkness means night forever. The clock is inside the fly.

items.p: Why might city birds sing higher notes than birds in quiet woods?
opts: So their songs can be heard over the low rumble of traffic
items.why: Traffic noise is mostly low and rumbly. Higher notes stand out above it. Scientists found this in great tits in the Dutch city of Leiden. Picking 'thinner air' invents a reason without evidence.

items.p: Scientists fully understand how migrating birds sense Earth's magnetism.
items.why: False. Birds seem to sense magnetism, but how is still argued about. One idea uses a substance in their eyes and a quantum effect. Nobody has proven it.

items.p: A friend says house sparrows are vanishing only because of phone towers. What is the best reply?
opts: You are right, it is proven.
There is no strong evidence for that. Fewer nesting holes and fewer insects may matter more.
Sparrows have never lived in cities.
items.why: Scientists have not found strong evidence that towers harm sparrows. Missing nesting holes in new buildings and fewer insects for chicks are other ideas with more support. A good reply weighs the evidence.

items.p: Sort these homes. Does the animal BUILD it, DIG it, or FIND it ready-made?
items: parakeet in an old tree hole
rat snake in a rat's old hole
items.why: Some animals build, some dig, and some move into homes made by others. A rat snake often takes over a burrow a rat dug.

items.p: Your diary shows a gecko by the tube light every night at 8 pm. When the light is off one night, the gecko is not there. What is the best next step?
opts: Test it: watch on more nights with the light on and off.
Say the gecko has moved away for ever.
items.why: One night is not enough. A scientist tests the idea again: light on some nights, off others. Picking 'hate the dark' jumps to a conclusion from one night.

items.p: Leopards live in Sanjay Gandhi National Park inside Mumbai. Some people want them all taken away. Others want people and leopards to share. Write what you think, and give one reason.
items.a: I think people and leopards can share, if people keep lights on at night, do not leave rubbish that attracts dogs, and keep children inside after dark. The leopards were there first, and taking them away might just let new ones come.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a view and a reason, and thinks about both people and leopards.

items.p: Why do you think many animals that do well in towns eat many kinds of food?
opts: Because towns offer a mix of foods that change often
Because towns have only one food
Because these animals never get hungry
Because food in towns is always healthy
items.why: Towns are full of scraps, insects at lights, fruit trees and grain. An animal that can eat many things can live on whatever is around. Animals that need one special food often cannot.

items.p: A weaver bird nest has blobs of mud inside. Which statement is honest?
opts: Scientists are sure it is to make the nest heavy.
It is a real puzzle. Scientists have ideas but are not sure why.
The mud is put there by people.
The mud is there by accident only.
items.why: The mud is real, but the reason is still argued about. Being honest means saying 'we do not know yet'.

items.p: A home can be made from things that came from other living things and from people.
items.why: True. A crow's nest is made from tree twigs, and in cities from wire and plastic that people made. A hornbill's sealed hole uses mud and droppings.

items.p: Put the steps of a good animal watch in order.
items: choose one animal you can find every day
watch at set times and write the time and what it did
look for things that happen again and again
say your claim, evidence and reasoning
items.why: This is how a naturalist finds a habit: same animal, set times, many days, then patterns, then a claim backed by evidence.

items.p: The scientist who began watching wild chimpanzees in Tanzania in 1960, before she had a university degree, is Jane ____.
items.why: Jane Goodall watched the same chimpanzees for years. That is how she saw them make and use tools.

items.p: Dung beetles in Africa can roll their balls in a straight line on moonless nights. What do they use?
opts: The light of the Milky Way
items.why: In 2013 scientists put tiny caps over the beetles' eyes and tested them in a planetarium. The beetles used the glow of the Milky Way to keep straight. Picking 'luck' ignores the evidence from the test.

items.p: Is a city a natural place? Give a reason for your answer.
items.a: Yes, in a way. Ants and termites build cities too, and we call those natural. People are animals, and many wild animals live in our cities. But a city is also very different from a forest, so some animals cannot live there.
items.why: This is a big question with no single answer. A good answer gives a reason and thinks about both sides.

items.p: Draw a timeline of one animal's day, from sunrise to night, using what you saw in My Animal Week.
items.a: A line from sunrise to night with drawings of what the animal did at each time, for example a crow calling at dawn, feeding in the morning, resting at noon and flying to its roost at sunset.
items.why: A timeline shows a habit at a glance. It is built from many days of watching.
items.art: A long empty arrow from a rising sun to a moon.

opts: Something an animal does again and again
quiz.why: A habit is a repeated behaviour, often at the same time or in the same place. Picking 'home' mixes up habit and habitat.

quiz.p: Which animal is diurnal, busy in the day?
quiz.why: Palm squirrels are busy all day and sleep at night. Owls, fruit bats and moths are mostly nocturnal.

quiz.p: Why are many animals in India quiet at noon?
opts: It is the hottest time, so they rest in the shade.
They are all asleep for the night.
They are eating all the time.
quiz.why: Noon is the hottest part of the day. Resting in the shade or in a burrow saves water and energy. Picking 'cannot see' is not true for most animals.

quiz.p: What is a crow's nest mainly for?
opts: Sleeping in every night of the year
quiz.why: Crows build nests to lay eggs and raise chicks. The rest of the year they sleep on branches at a roost. Thinking birds live in nests all year is a common mistake.

quiz.p: Which home is woven from strips of grass?
quiz.why: The baya weaver tears long strips of grass and weaves a hanging nest. Bees build with wax, rats dig, and termites build with soil.

quiz.p: Which animal lives in Sanjay Gandhi National Park, inside the city of Mumbai?
quiz.why: Leopards live in this park and sometimes walk past homes at night. Snow leopards live high in the Himalayas. Polar bears and kangaroos do not live in India in the wild.

quiz.p: Why do black kites circle over Delhi's markets?
opts: They are migrating to the sea.
quiz.why: Markets have meat and food scraps. Kites have learned that markets mean food. Picking 'lost' assumes wild animals do not belong in cities.

quiz.p: You want to find out when your pigeons are busiest. What should you do?
opts: Watch at set times for a week and write down what they do.
quiz.why: Habits show up only when you watch many times and write things down. One look shows just one moment.

quiz.p: In the Busy Times test, what was the one thing we changed?
quiz.why: In a fair test we change only one thing. Here it was the time of day. Everything else stayed the same.

quiz.p: In the Ant Trail Test, the ants walked on under a hand held above the trail. But they stopped and wandered where the floor was rubbed. What is the best claim?
opts: Ants follow something on the floor, and rubbing removed it.
Ants can only walk in straight lines.
Ants stop wherever a person has been.
quiz.why: The hand above the trail changed little, so the hand was not the cause. Rubbing took away the smell trail, a chemical called a pheromone, that the ants were following. Picking 'scared of hands' does not fit what we saw, because the ants walked on under the hand.

quiz.p: You find a nest with eggs in a bush. What should you do?
opts: Pick up an egg to look closely.
Watch from a distance and leave it alone.
Take the nest home to keep it safe.
Shake the bush to see the bird.
quiz.why: Touching or moving a nest can make the parents leave the eggs. We watch kindly, from far away.

quiz.p: How do migrating birds sense Earth's magnetism?
opts: Scientists know exactly, it is fully proven.
Scientists have ideas, such as a substance in their eyes, but it is not fully proven.
Birds cannot sense magnetism at all.
quiz.why: Birds do seem to sense magnetism, but how is still an open question. Being honest about what we do not know is part of science.

quiz.p: Why do rock pigeons nest on ledges of tall buildings?
opts: Ledges are like the cliffs their wild relatives used.
quiz.why: Wild rock pigeons nest on cliff ledges. To a pigeon, a building is a cliff. Picking 'cannot build' is wrong. Pigeons build simple twig nests.

quiz.p: Which of these is a fact from an animal diary, not a guess?
opts: At 2 pm the dog slept in the shade of the gate.
The dog wants to be my friend.
The dog is the oldest in the street.
quiz.why: A fact has something anyone could see, with a time. Feelings and ages are guesses unless we have more evidence.

applications: Bird counts like the Great Backyard Bird Count use families' watching to track India's birds.
Wildlife scientists use camera traps that photograph animals at night to learn their habits.
Dengue mosquitoes bite mostly in the day, especially in the early morning and late afternoon. Malaria mosquitoes bite mostly at night. Knowing these habits helps people protect themselves.
Farmers time their work around animal habits, such as when birds eat ripening grain.
Architects copy termite mounds to design buildings that stay cool with less electricity.
Cities plan wildlife corridors, safe paths for animals between parks.
Forest departments use animal habits to plan where to put water holes in summer.
Pest control works better when it follows the habits of rats and cockroaches, such as cleaning food away at night.
Bird nest boxes help house sparrows where new buildings have no holes.
Airports study bird habits to keep birds away from planes at take-off.
Lights that face downwards help night insects and birds in cities.

open_questions.q: Why are house sparrows disappearing from some Indian cities but not others?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have several ideas, such as fewer nesting holes and fewer insects, but the evidence is mixed and differs from city to city.

open_questions.q: How exactly do birds sense Earth's magnetism to find their way?
open_questions.why_open: There are two main ideas, and experiments support parts of each. Nobody has seen the sense working inside a living bird.

open_questions.q: Why do baya weaver birds put mud inside their nests?
open_questions.why_open: The mud is real, but nobody has tested the ideas well enough to be sure.

open_questions.q: Are city animals changing in their bodies and genes, not only in their habits?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies suggest yes, but changes take many generations, and it is hard to tell learned habits from inherited ones.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of animals live in a single Indian city?
open_questions.why_open: Birds are well counted, but insects, spiders and soil animals are not. Many have not even been named.

open_questions.q: Does an animal know its home is its home, the way we do?
open_questions.why_open: We can see that animals return to their homes and defend them. What they feel about them is very hard to test.

open_questions.q: How do termites know how to build a mound much bigger than any one of them?
open_questions.why_open: Each termite follows simple rules, and the mound grows from all of them together. Scientists are still working out the rules.
