maths.problem: In the Busy Times test, a child made these tally marks over 3 days. Morning: 14 visits. Noon: 3 visits. Evening: 11 visits. How many more birds came in the morning than at noon?
maths.explain: Morning had 14 visits. Noon had 3. 14 take away 3 is 11. So 11 more birds came in the morning than at noon.
maths.context: This is about the Busy Times test. You put out a bowl of water and counted how many birds landed in 10 minutes, at three times of day, for three days.

chart.title: Bird visits to a water bowl over 3 days

maths.why_maths: Taking one number from another tells us how big the difference is, so we can say how much busier one time is, not just that it is busier.

maths.problem: Here are the tally marks from the Busy Times test: morning, two groups of five and four more. How many visits is that?
maths.explain: Each group of five tally marks is 5. Two groups make 5 + 5 = 10. Four more lines make 10 + 4 = 14.
maths.context: This is about the Busy Times test, where you drew one tally line every time a bird landed at a water bowl.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks let you count quickly while you watch. Grouping in fives makes the total easy to add up afterwards.

maths.problem: In My Animal Week you watched your animal for 10 minutes a day for 7 days. How many minutes did you watch in all?
maths.explain: 7 days of 10 minutes is 7 groups of 10. 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 = 70. Or 7 × 10 = 70. That is 1 hour and 10 minutes.
maths.context: This is about My Animal Week, the project where you watched one animal near your home for about 10 minutes every day for a week.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how small daily watches add up to a long study, which is how naturalists collect enough evidence.

maths.problem: In the Cool Home Test, the thermometer read 44 °C on open ground in the sun, 35 °C in the shade and 30 °C inside the hole. How much cooler was the hole than the open ground? How much cooler was the shade?
maths.answer: The hole was 14 degrees cooler. The shade was 9 degrees cooler.
maths.explain: 44 take away 30 is 14. So the hole was 14 degrees cooler than the open ground. 44 take away 35 is 9. So the shade was 9 degrees cooler. The hole was the best place for an animal to rest.
maths.context: This is about the Cool Home Test. You measured how hot it was on open ground in the sun, in the shade, and inside a little hole in the soil, like a burrow.

chart.title: Temperature after 5 minutes in each place

maths.why_maths: Subtracting the temperatures tells us exactly how much cooler a burrow is, which shows why it is such a good place to hide at noon.

maths.problem: In the Ant Trail Test, a child counted the ants crossing one spot in 1 minute. Before rubbing: 12 ants. First minute after rubbing: 2 ants. Third minute after rubbing: 9 ants. How many fewer ants crossed just after rubbing? About how many would you expect in the fifth minute, and why?
maths.answer: 10 fewer ants crossed just after rubbing. In the fifth minute you would expect about 12 again, because the ants are laying the trail again.
maths.explain: 12 take away 2 is 10, so 10 fewer ants crossed just after rubbing. From 2 to 9 is a rise of 7 in two minutes. The numbers are climbing back towards 12, the number before we rubbed. So a good guess for the fifth minute is about 12, once the smell trail is back.
maths.context: This is about the Ant Trail Test. You counted ants crossing one spot on their trail, then rubbed away a short piece of the trail and counted again.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the counts shows how much rubbing changed the trail, and the pattern over time lets us predict when the trail will be back to normal.

roots.context: We have been watching the animals around us: when they are busy, where they live, and how ants keep to one path. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: An ant that has never been to the sugar can still find it. It follows the scent that other ants left on the floor. Rub the scent away and the path is lost until ants lay it again. So part of what the ants know is kept on the floor they share, not only inside each ant.
deep_truth.habit: We think whatever an animal knows must be stored inside its own head. An ant trail shows a colony keeping its way to food outside any one body, on the ground, where every ant can follow it and add to it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Ant Trail Test, ants walked on under a hand held above the trail, but stopped and wandered where the floor was rubbed. A few minutes later the line formed again.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal too. You have habits, a home and a body clock, like the crow outside.
three.what_is_life: Living things make homes from what is near, like twigs and mud, and from what their bodies make, like wax and silk. City crows even use our lost hair clips.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is one big shared home. Every wall, tree and drain is somebody's house.

roots.thread: The crows' nest in the story was made of a neem tree, a family's lost wire and two crows' work. An ant trail is made by hundreds of ants, each adding a little scent. Neither belongs to one maker. One awareness runs through the whole world and shows itself in countless separate lives. A nest or a trail is a small, real picture of that: many lives making one thing together.

teachings.teaching: Everything in this moving world is filled with the one Lord. Enjoy it by letting go, and do not grab what belongs to anyone.
teachings.link: Our building is also the pigeons' cliff and the gecko's hunting ground. The verse asks us to take what we need and leave room for others, which is how we try to share a building with crows and pigeons.

science.text: People and all other animals share one family tree. We are animals, related to the crow and the ant.
Many kinds of ants lay scent trails with chemicals called pheromones. Other ants follow them, and a trail fades unless ants keep adding to it.

other_view.who: René Descartes, a French philosopher, and many scientists today
other_view.view: Descartes wrote in 1637 that animals work like machines, without thought. Many scientists today would say an ant trail is only chemistry: each ant reacts to a smell, and nothing in the trail knows anything.

practice.title: Count the neighbours
practice.say: Let's sit very still and close our eyes. For one minute, just listen. Each time you hear an animal, quietly lift one finger. Now open your eyes and count your fingers. Now listen once more, to your own breath going in and out. You are one more animal, breathing in this place. Who else is breathing here with us?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Listen for one minute. Lift a finger for each animal you hear. Then listen to your own breath.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people believed that only humans make tools. One famous book even called humans 'man the tool-maker', as if making tools was what set us apart from every other animal. In July 1960, Jane Goodall, a 26-year-old English woman with no university degree, went to Gombe in Tanzania to watch wild chimpanzees. Louis Leakey, a scientist who studied human ancestors, had sent her. For months the chimpanzees ran away whenever she came near. She kept coming back to the same places, quietly, day after day. Late in 1960 she saw a chimpanzee she called David Greybeard push a grass stem into a termite mound and pull it out covered in termites. Later she saw chimpanzees strip the leaves off twigs to make better probes. That is making a tool. Leakey wrote back: 'Now we must redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.' Goodall saw it only because she watched the same animals, patiently, for a very long time.
how_we_found_out.who: Jane Goodall, sent to Gombe by Louis Leakey
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Only humans make and use tools. Goodall saw wild chimpanzees making tools from twigs and grass stems, by watching them for months.
